title: How Ghost Prisons Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss CIA "ghost prisons" (secret black-site prisons) and extraordinary rendition after September 11, 2001. They cover the Bush Senior-era rendition finding, the expansion of rendition after 2001, the New York Times estimate of at least 307 renditions, secret prison sites such as Salt Pit near Kabul (a detainee froze to death there), Thailand and Eastern Europe host countries, Sven Maso-style investigation of CIA-chartered Gulfstream planes, the Physicians for Human Rights report on medical involvement in enhanced interrogation, torture-related music, and Obama closing the network in January 2009. The episode closes with a listener-mail style recap of the hosts' New York live show, including a happy hour at the Knitting Factory with The Onion and a trivia night with guests including John Hodgman and Ira Glass.
topics: stuff you should know live New York

segments.title: Opening banter and studio move
segments.summary: Hosts joke about their new studio, the absence of producer Jerry, and a sponsor read for GoToMeeting before introducing the topic of post-9/11 blame and the Clinton-era CIA target list.

segments.title: Target list and extraordinary rendition origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the CIA target list of al Qaeda figures passed along before September 11 and the debate over assassination. They explain that extraordinary rendition began under the first Bush presidency via a secret presidential finding, and was used a couple dozen times mainly in the Clinton era to bring terrorists to US courts.

segments.title: Expansion of rendition after 2001
segments.summary: After 2001 the CIA shifted rendition toward third-party countries to outsource interrogation and torture, bypassing US courts and habeas corpus. The New York Times estimated at least 307 renditions between late 2001 and 2005.

segments.title: Ghost prisons and CIA denial
segments.summary: The CIA set up a network of secret prisons known as ghost prisons, with detainees called ghost prisoners. Human Rights Watch and ProPublica tracked suspected cases. The CIA long refused to acknowledge the prisons until President George W. Bush admitted their existence in 2006. Obama shut the network down in January 2009, though groups say dozens remain unaccounted for.

segments.title: Deaths in custody and Salt Pit
segments.summary: The hosts discuss detainees who may have died in custody, citing a container transport in Afghanistan and the Salt Pit site in a brick factory near Kabul where a detainee froze to death. Secret prison code names are discussed, including Camp Dark Prison and Camp Bond Steel.

segments.title: Legal rights, Red Cross access, and host countries
segments.summary: The hosts compare detainee rights at Guantanamo and under the Geneva Convention with the secret prisons, where the Red Cross was denied access. They list host countries including Thailand, Eastern European states such as Lithuania, Romania and Bulgaria, and others, and discuss how they were kept secret even from host governments.

segments.title: Gulfstream flights, Sven Mörk investigation, and torture-related physicians
segments.summary: A Swedish TV producer traced CIA-chartered Gulfstream jets, reportedly finding dozens of flights; the hosts discuss the flight manifests and dummy companies. They also discuss the Physicians for Human Rights report on physicians involved in enhanced interrogation and a January 2010 joint study on the fate of detainees, and the Abu Zubaydah case and music used in interrogations.

segments.title: Sign-off and live show recap
segments.summary: After a brief mention of further reading and a New York live show recap covering a Brooklyn happy hour and trivia night, the hosts invite listener suggestions for future cities and sign off with a sponsor line.
